short_definition: Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) is the percentage of your gross monthly income that goes toward monthly debt payments, and lenders use it to judge whether you can afford a new loan.
explanation: To calculate your debt-to-income ratio, add up your required monthly debt payments, such as a mortgage, car loan, student loan, personal loan and minimum credit card payments. Divide that total by your gross (pre-tax) monthly income and multiply by 100. Everyday costs like groceries and utilities are usually left out. Some lenders also look at a 'front-end' ratio that counts only housing costs.

Debt-to-income ratio matters because it is one of the main numbers lenders check, along with your credit score, when deciding whether to approve a mortgage or loan and on what terms. A lower DTI generally points to more room in your budget. Lenders' limits vary by country, loan type and lender, so ask the lender which ratio and method they use.

Debt-to-income ratio is a blunt measure. It is based on gross income, so it ignores taxes and local living costs, and it says nothing about your savings. A DTI that a lender will accept can still feel tight in real life, so also check affordability against your actual take-home budget.
example: Illustrative example: your gross monthly income is $5,000. Your monthly debt payments are a $1,200 mortgage, a $300 car loan and $100 in minimum card payments, for a total of $1,600. Your DTI is $1,600 ÷ $5,000 = 32%. Paying off the car loan would lower it to $1,300 ÷ $5,000 = 26%.
common_mistake: Calculating DTI from take-home pay instead of gross income, or confusing it with credit utilization (how much of your credit limits you are using). Either way you end up with a different number from the one lenders typically use.
title: Debt-to-Income Ratio (DTI)
